means:
Behaviour or speech adopted **for effect** — striking an attitude to impress, intimidate, or signal a position you don't actually intend to act on.

The word is an accusation of hollowness. Calling a threat *posturing* says the speaker is performing toughness with no intention of following through; calling a principled stand *posturing* says the principle is a costume. It's cooler and more dismissive than *grandstanding* (loud, attention-hungry) and more strategic than *pretending* — a posturer usually wants something out of the pose, typically leverage.
trick_line: **Posture** is a position you *hold on purpose* — posturing is holding a moral position the same way: consciously, for the room, and only until you can relax.
trick_unpack: Nobody's straight back at a dinner table is natural, and neither is the outrage of a politician who knows the cameras are on.
sentences: The ultimatum was dismissed by every analyst as **posturing**, calculated to extract concessions before the deadline rather than to precipitate a war.
Ignore him — all that gym-bro chest-thumping is just **posturing**, he'd run a mile from an actual fight.
in_the_wild: **\"Political posturing\"** is one of the most-used phrases in news writing — any time a correspondent says a bill, a walkout, or a threat was \"mere posturing,\" they mean it was theatre staged for voters, not governing.
etymology:
Latin **pōnere / positus** = *"to place, to put."* A **posture** is literally how you've placed your body; posturing is placing yourself in a stance for an audience.

Same root, whole GRE family: **position, posit, deposit, compose, impose, juxtapose, repository**.
one_line: Striking an attitude for effect, with no intention behind it.
